problems.title: An epsilon proof for a reciprocal sequence
problems.objective: Prove convergence directly from the epsilon definition.
problems.statement: Using only the definition of sequence convergence, prove that $a_n=1/(n+1)$ converges to $0$.
problems.strategy: Given ε>0, choose an integer N with N+1>1/ε. Then for n≥N, compare n+1 with N+1 and invert the positive inequality. Finally, conclude |1/(n+1)-0|<ε with one N working for every n≥N.
hints: Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose an integer $N$ with $N+1>1/\varepsilon$.
For $n\ge N$, compare $n+1$ with $N+1$ and invert the positive inequality.
Conclude $|1/(n+1)-0|<\varepsilon$ with one $N$ working for every $n\ge N$.
problems.solution: Let $\varepsilon>0$. By the Archimedean property choose $N\in \mathbb N$ with $N+1>1/\varepsilon$. If $n\ge N$, then $n+1\ge N+1>1/\varepsilon$, so $0<1/(n+1)<\varepsilon$. Hence $|a_n-0|<\varepsilon$ for every $n\ge N$, proving $a_n\to 0$.
rubricCriteria: Correctly carries out the first key step: Given ε>0, choose an integer N with N+1>1/ε.
Justifies the central transition: For n≥N, compare n+1 with N+1 and invert the positive inequality.
Completes the requested conclusion: Conclude |1/(n+1)-0|<ε with one N working for every n≥N.

commonErrors.description: Choosing the cutoff as $N=n$, so the threshold depends on the tail index instead of only on $\varepsilon$.
commonErrors.consequence: This invalidates the central inference or leaves a required case unjustified.

commonErrors.description: Choosing N after fixing n, thereby reversing the quantifier order.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated conclusion no longer follows from the argument as written.

problems.flawedProof: Fix ε>0 and for each n choose N=n; then n≥N and 1/(n+1)<ε eventually. Thus the sequence converges. The choice N=n is illegal because N must depend only on ε and work for all later n.

problems.title: Two parity limits determine the whole limit
problems.objective: Reassemble convergence of a sequence from convergence of its even and odd subsequences.
problems.statement: Suppose $a_{2k}\to L$ and $a_{2k+1}\to L$. Prove directly that $a_n\to L$.
permittedResults: Every natural number is even or odd
problems.strategy: First obtain convergence cutoffs for the even and odd subsequences. Then choose an original-index cutoff that forces the associated parity index beyond the relevant threshold. Finally split an arbitrary late $n$ into its even or odd form and apply the matching estimate.
hints: Choose separate cutoffs for $a_{2k}$ and $a_{2k+1}$.
Convert a large original index $n$ into a sufficiently large parity index $k$.
Use one original cutoff large enough for both parity cases.
problems.solution: Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $K_e,K_o$ so $k\ge K_e$ implies $|a_{2k}-L|<\varepsilon$ and $k\ge K_o$ implies $|a_{2k+1}-L|<\varepsilon$. Let $K=\max(K_e,K_o)$ and $N=2K+1$. If $n\ge N$, write either $n=2k$ or $n=2k+1$. In the even case $2k\ge2K+1$ forces $k\ge K+1$; in the odd case $2k+1\ge2K+1$ gives $k\ge K$. Thus the appropriate parity estimate gives $|a_n-L|<\varepsilon$. Hence $a_n\to L$.
rubricCriteria: Chooses valid convergence cutoffs for both parity subsequences.
Relates every sufficiently large original index to a sufficiently large parity index.
Handles both parity cases and concludes the epsilon definition for the full sequence.

commonErrors.description: Assuming the two parity subsequences use the same cutoff without taking a maximum.
commonErrors.consequence: This invalidates the decisive inference or leaves a required case unjustified.

commonErrors.description: Writing that every large index is even, or failing to handle one parity.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated conclusion no longer follows from the argument as written.

problems.flawedProof: Every term lies in either the even or odd subsequence, and both subsequences converge to $L$, so the result is immediate. This omits the uniform tail argument: one must show a single original cutoff makes the relevant parity index large in both cases.

problems.title: A nonzero limit fixes the eventual sign
problems.objective: Turn convergence to a nonzero value into a uniform eventual sign conclusion.
problems.statement: Suppose $a_n\to L$ with $L\ne0$. Prove that $a_nL>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$, and deduce $|a_n|\ge |L|/2$ eventually.
permittedResults: Order properties of the real numbers
problems.strategy: Choose half the nonzero limiting magnitude as the convergence tolerance. Use the resulting interval around $L$ to show late terms have the same sign as $L$. Then apply the reverse triangle inequality to obtain the quantitative lower bound.
hints: Use the tolerance $\varepsilon=|L|/2$.
The estimate $|a_n-L|<|L|/2$ prevents $a_n$ from crossing zero.
Apply $|a_n|\ge |L|-|a_n-L|$ for the magnitude bound.
problems.solution: Because $L\ne0$, $\varepsilon=|L|/2>0$. Choose $N$ so $n\ge N$ implies $|a_n-L|<|L|/2$. If $L>0$, then $a_n>L-|L|/2=L/2>0$; if $L<0$, then $a_n<L+|L|/2=L/2<0$. Hence $a_nL>0$ eventually. Moreover, the reverse triangle inequality gives $|a_n|\ge |L|-|a_n-L|>|L|/2$ for every $n\ge N$.
rubricCriteria: Uses the positive tolerance $|L|/2$ under the hypothesis $L\ne 0$.
Separates the cases $L>0$ and $L<0$ or gives an equivalent sign argument.
Derives the eventual lower bound using the reverse triangle inequality.

problems.title: Limits commute with finite maxima
problems.objective: Prove convergence of a pointwise maximum without assuming one branch is eventually dominant.
problems.statement: Suppose $a_n\to A$ and $b_n\to B$. Prove that $\max\{a_n,b_n\}\to\max\{A,B\}$, including the tied case $A=B$.
problems.strategy: Rewrite the maximum using addition and absolute value, pass each component through the limit, and identify the resulting expression as the maximum of the two limits. This avoids an invalid eventual-dominance case split when the limits tie.
hints: Verify $\max\{x,y\}=(x+y+|x-y|)/2$ for arbitrary real $x,y$.
Use $a_n-b_n\to A-B$ and the reverse triangle inequality to pass absolute values through the limit.
Combine the component limits and rewrite the result as $\max\{A,B\}$.
problems.solution: For every $n$, $$\max\{a_n,b_n\}=\frac{a_n+b_n+|a_n-b_n|}{2}.$$ Limit algebra gives $a_n+b_n\to A+B$ and $a_n-b_n\to A-B$. The reverse triangle inequality then yields $|a_n-b_n|\to|A-B|$. Therefore the displayed expression converges to $(A+B+|A-B|)/2=\max\{A,B\}$. This argument also covers $A=B$, when neither branch need eventually dominate.
rubricCriteria: States and correctly applies the algebraic identity for the maximum.
Justifies convergence of the absolute-value difference using a valid inequality.
Combines the limits and explicitly handles the tied-limit case.

commonErrors.description: Choosing the eventually larger branch from the limits even when the two limiting values are equal.
commonErrors.consequence: When $A=B$, the two branches may cross infinitely often, so the proposed eventual case split is unavailable.

commonErrors.description: Using the maximum identity but passing absolute value through the limit without justification.
commonErrors.consequence: The decisive component limit remains unproved.

problems.flawedProof: If $A>B$, eventually $a_n>b_n$, and if $B>A$, eventually $b_n>a_n$; therefore the maximum converges to the larger limit. When $A=B$, choose either branch as eventually larger and argue the same way. The final step is false: two sequences with the same limit can cross infinitely often, so no branch need be eventually maximal.

problems.title: A subsequence criterion for convergence
problems.objective: Characterize convergence by the behavior of further subsequences.
problems.statement: Prove that $a_n\to L$ if and only if every subsequence $(a_{n_k})$ has a further subsequence converging to $L$.
permittedResults: Subsequences of convergent sequences converge to the same limit
problems.strategy: For the easy direction, pass the known limit through a subsequence and then a further subsequence. For the converse, use the quantified negation of convergence to construct a subsequence that remains uniformly separated from $L$. Observe that none of its further subsequences can converge to $L$.
hints: The forward implication follows by applying subsequence inheritance twice.
If $a_n\not\to L$, fix $\varepsilon_0>0$ and recursively choose bad indices $n_k$.
Every further subsequence of the bad subsequence stays at least $\varepsilon_0$ from $L$.
problems.solution: If $a_n\to L$, every subsequence converges to $L$, so any further subsequence does as well. Conversely, suppose $a_n\not\to L$. Then some $\varepsilon_0>0$ has the property that after every cutoff there is an index $n$ with $|a_n-L|\ge\varepsilon_0$. Recursively choose $n_{k+1}>n_k$ with this property. The resulting subsequence stays at distance at least $\varepsilon_0$ from $L$, and every further subsequence has the same property; therefore no further subsequence converges to $L$. This contradicts the assumed criterion, so $a_n\to L$.
rubricCriteria: Proves the forward implication using subsequence inheritance.
Constructs a strictly increasing bad-index subsequence from the negation of convergence.
Shows no further subsequence of the constructed sequence can converge to $L$.

commonErrors.description: Replacing “every subsequence has a further subsequence converging to $L$” by the stronger and unjustified claim that every subsequence converges to $L$.
commonErrors.consequence: This invalidates the decisive inference or leaves a required case unjustified.

commonErrors.description: Choosing bad indices without ensuring they increase strictly.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated conclusion no longer follows from the argument as written.

problems.flawedProof: If every subsequence has one further subsequence converging to $L$, then every subsequence converges to $L$, so the original sequence converges. The first implication is false: existence of one good further subsequence does not make the whole subsequence converge; the contrapositive construction is essential.

problems.title: Decreasing convergence via the infimum
problems.objective: Prove the decreasing bounded-below case of monotone convergence using a greatest lower bound.
problems.statement: Let $(a_n)$ be decreasing and bounded below. Prove $a_n\to \inf\{a_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$.
problems.strategy: Use the infimum rather than reflecting the already-proved increasing theorem. Find one term below $L+\varepsilon$ because that number is not a lower bound. Then use decreasingness and the lower-bound property to trap the entire tail.
hints: Let $L=\inf\{a_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ and note that $L+\varepsilon$ is not a lower bound.
Choose $N$ with $L\le a_N<L+\varepsilon$.
For $n\ge N$, decreasingness traps $a_n$ between $L$ and $L+\varepsilon$.
problems.solution: Let $L=\inf\{a_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, $L+\varepsilon$ cannot be a lower bound of the range, or it would exceed the greatest lower bound. Hence some $N$ satisfies $a_N<L+\varepsilon$. If $n\ge N$, decreasingness gives $a_n\le a_N$, while the lower-bound property gives $L\le a_n$. Thus $L\le a_n<L+\varepsilon$, so $|a_n-L|<\varepsilon$. Therefore $a_n\to L$.
rubricCriteria: Defines the candidate limit as the infimum and uses its lower-bound property.
Uses failure of $L+\varepsilon$ to be a lower bound to choose $N$.
Applies decreasingness in the correct direction to trap the tail.

commonErrors.consequence: This invalidates the decisive inference or leaves a required case unjustified.

commonErrors.description: Using decreasingness backward and writing $a_N\le a_n$ for $n\ge N$.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated conclusion no longer follows from the argument as written.

problems.flawedProof: Choose $N$ with $a_N=L$ because $L$ is the infimum. Then all later terms equal $L$. An infimum need not be attained, and even an attained lower bound does not by itself force every later term to be equal without using monotonicity carefully.

problems.title: A recursively averaged sequence
problems.objective: Analyze monotonicity and convergence of a nonlinear recurrence.
problems.statement: Let $a_1=2$ and $a_{n+1}=(a_n+3/a_n)/2$. Prove $a_n\ge \sqrt{3}$, prove it is decreasing, and find its limit.
problems.strategy: Use AM-GM to show the recurrence sends positive terms to values at least √3. Then rewrite a_{n+1}-a_n=(3-a_n²)/(2a_n) and determine its sign. Finally, pass to the limit in 2a_{n+1}=a_n+3/a_n and select the positive root.
hints: Use AM-GM to show the recurrence sends positive terms to values at least $\sqrt{3}$.
Rewrite $a_{n+1}-a_n=(3-a_n^2)/(2a_n)$ and determine its sign.
Pass to the limit in $2a_{n+1}=a_n+3/a_n$ and select the positive root.
problems.solution: All terms are positive, and AM-GM gives $a_{n+1}\ge \sqrt{a_n\cdot 3/a_n}=\sqrt{3}$. Since $a_n\ge \sqrt{3}$, $a_{n+1}-a_n=(3-a_n^2)/(2a_n)\le 0$. Thus $(a_n)$ decreases and is bounded below, so $a_n\to L\ge \sqrt{3}$. Passing to the recurrence yields $2L=L+3/L$, hence $L^2=3$ and $L=\sqrt{3}$.
rubricCriteria: Correctly carries out the first key step: Use AM-GM to show the recurrence sends positive terms to values at least √3.
Justifies the central transition: Rewrite a_{n+1}-a_n=(3-a_n²)/(2a_n) and determine its sign.
Completes the requested conclusion: Pass to the limit in 2a_{n+1}=a_n+3/a_n and select the positive root.

problems.title: Summable increments force sequence convergence
problems.objective: Turn absolute summability of successive changes into a Cauchy estimate for the sequence.
problems.statement: Suppose $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|a_{n+1}-a_n|$ converges. Prove $(a_n)$ converges, and show that for $m>n$, $$|a_m-a_n|\le\sum_{k=n}^{m-1}|a_{k+1}-a_k|.$$
problems.strategy: Telescope $a_m-a_n$ into successive increments and apply the finite-sum triangle inequality. Use convergence of the absolute-increment series to make every sufficiently late increment tail small. This is exactly the Cauchy condition for $(a_n)$, so completeness supplies a limit.
hints: For $m>n$, write $a_m-a_n=\sum_{k=n}^{m-1}(a_{k+1}-a_k)$.
Apply the finite-sum triangle inequality to obtain the requested bound.
Use the Cauchy tail criterion for $\sum|a_{n+1}-a_n|$, then completeness of $\mathbb R$.
problems.solution: For $m>n$, telescoping gives $$a_m-a_n=\sum_{k=n}^{m-1}(a_{k+1}-a_k).$$ Therefore the finite-sum triangle inequality yields $$|a_m-a_n|\le\sum_{k=n}^{m-1}|a_{k+1}-a_k|.$$ Given $\varepsilon>0$, convergence of $\sum|a_{k+1}-a_k|$ supplies $N$ such that every finite tail beginning at $n\ge N$ is below $\varepsilon$. Hence $m>n\ge N$ implies $|a_m-a_n|<\varepsilon$; the case $m=n$ is immediate, and the opposite order follows by symmetry. Thus $(a_n)$ is Cauchy and consequently converges in $\mathbb R$.
rubricCriteria: Writes the exact telescoping identity for $a_m-a_n$.
Derives the requested bound with the finite-sum triangle inequality.
Uses small tails of the convergent increment series to prove the Cauchy condition and invokes completeness.

commonErrors.description: Concluding that $(a_n)$ is Cauchy merely because $a_{n+1}-a_n\to0$.
commonErrors.consequence: Vanishing individual increments do not control their accumulated tail; harmonic partial sums are a counterexample.

commonErrors.description: Telescoping the signed increments but replacing the absolute value of their sum by equality with the sum of absolute values.
commonErrors.consequence: Only the triangle inequality is valid when increments can have different signs.

problems.flawedProof: Convergence of $\sum|a_{n+1}-a_n|$ implies $a_{n+1}-a_n\to0$. Therefore all sufficiently late neighboring terms are close, so by transitivity every pair of late terms is close and $(a_n)$ is Cauchy. Closeness does not pass through arbitrarily long chains without accumulating error; the summable-tail estimate is the decisive step.

problems.title: A geometric sequence under the unit threshold
problems.objective: Prove r^n→0 for |r|<1 with a quantitative argument.
problems.statement: Let $r\in \mathbb R$ with $|r|<1$. Prove $r^n\to 0$.
problems.strategy: Reduce to q=|r| and handle q=0 separately. Then for 0<q<1 write q=1/(1+c) with c>0 and use (1+c)^n≥1+nc. Finally, choose n so 1/(1+nc)<ε and transfer the estimate to |r^n|.
hints: Reduce to $q=|r|$ and handle $q=0$ separately.
For $0<q<1$ write $q=1/(1+c)$ with $c>0$ and use $(1+c)^n\ge 1+nc$.
Choose $n$ so $1/(1+nc)<\varepsilon$ and transfer the estimate to $|r^n|$.
problems.solution: If $r=0$ the claim is immediate. Otherwise $q=|r|\in (0,1)$, so $q=1/(1+c)$ for $c=1/q-1>0$. Bernoulli gives $(1+c)^n\ge 1+nc$, hence $|r^n|=q^n\le 1/(1+nc)$. The Archimedean property supplies $N$ with $1/(1+Nc)<\varepsilon$, and the same holds for $n\ge N$.
rubricCriteria: Correctly carries out the first key step: Reduce to q=|r| and handle q=0 separately.
Justifies the central transition: For 0<q<1 write q=1/(1+c) with c>0 and use (1+c)^n≥1+nc.
Completes the requested conclusion: Choose n so 1/(1+nc)<ε and transfer the estimate to |r^n|.

problems.objective: Prove basic algebra of continuous functions from epsilon-delta estimates.
problems.statement: If $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $a$ and $c\in \mathbb R$, prove $f+g$ and $cf$ are continuous at $a$.
problems.strategy: For f+g, request ε/2 control from each function and take the smaller delta. Then use the triangle inequality for the sum difference. Finally, for cf, handle c=0 separately and otherwise request ε/|c| control from f.

Use the triangle inequality for the sum difference.
For $cf$, handle $c=0$ separately and otherwise request $\varepsilon/|c|$ control from $f$.
problems.solution: Given $\varepsilon>0$, continuity gives $\delta_f,\delta_g$ for error $\varepsilon/2$. Justifies the central transition: Use the triangle inequality for the sum difference.

problems.objective: Pass a shared global modulus through uniform convergence.
problems.statement: Suppose $f_n:E\to\mathbb R$ are all $L$-Lipschitz for one constant $L\ge0$, and $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$. Prove $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz and hence uniformly continuous.
problems.strategy: For fixed inputs, insert and subtract one uniformly close approximating function. Use its common Lipschitz bound for the middle term and uniform convergence for both outer terms. Since the auxiliary error is arbitrary, remove it to recover the same constant.

problems.solution: Fix $x,y\in E$ and $\eta>0$. Uniform convergence gives $n$ such that $|f_n(z)-f(z)|<\eta$ for every $z\in E$. problems.title: Affine homeomorphism between compact intervals
problems.objective: Construct a continuous bijection with continuous inverse between two nondegenerate compact intervals.
problems.statement: For $a<b$ and $c<d$, define an explicit homeomorphism $[a,b]\to [c,d]$ and prove all required properties.
problems.strategy: Use h(x)=c+(d-c)(x-a)/(b-a). Then check h(a)=c, h(b)=d, and strict increase, giving bijectivity onto [c,d]. Finally, solve for x to write a continuous affine inverse.
hints: Use $h(x)=c+(d-c)(x-a)/(b-a)$.
Check $h(a)=c$, $h(b)=d$, and strict increase, giving bijectivity onto $[c,d]$.
Solve for $x$ to write a continuous affine inverse.
problems.solution: Define $h(x)=c+(d-c)(x-a)/(b-a)$. Positive slopes make $h$ strictly increasing, and its endpoint values are $c,d$, so it maps $[a,b]$ bijectively onto $[c,d]$. Solving $y=h(x)$ gives $h^{-1}(y)=a+(b-a)(y-c)/(d-c)$, also affine and continuous. Hence $h$ is a homeomorphism.

problems.title: A nontrivial connected subset of the line is uncountable
problems.objective: Use the interval property to deduce a cardinality consequence of connectedness.
problems.statement: Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R$ be connected and suppose $x,z\in E$ with $x<z$. Prove $[x,z]\subseteq E$ and conclude that $E$ is uncountable.
permittedResults: Connected subsets of $\mathbb R$ have the interval property
Every nondegenerate real interval is uncountable
problems.strategy: Apply the interval property to every point between the two given points, obtaining an entire nondegenerate closed interval inside $E$. Then transfer uncountability from that interval to $E$.
hints: Fix an arbitrary $y\in[x,z]$ and use connectedness together with $x,z\in E$.
Conclude $[x,z]\subseteq E$, including both endpoints.
Use $x<z$ to invoke uncountability of the nondegenerate interval.
problems.solution: Connected subsets of the real line have the interval property: whenever they contain two points, they contain every point between them. Thus for arbitrary $y\in[x,z]$, the endpoint assumptions give $y\in E$, so $[x,z]\subseteq E$. Because $x<z$, the interval $[x,z]$ is nondegenerate and uncountable. A set containing an uncountable subset is uncountable, hence $E$ is uncountable.
rubricCriteria: Applies the interval property to an arbitrary point of $[x,z]$.
Proves the full set inclusion, including the endpoints.
Uses nondegeneracy to transfer uncountability to $E$.

problems.objective: Combine compactness and connectedness preservation to classify an image.
problems.statement: Let $K\subset \mathbb R$ be nonempty, compact, and connected, and $f:K\to \mathbb R$ continuous. Prove $f(K)=[m,M]$ for some $m\le M$.

A nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb R$ has a minimum $m$ and maximum $M$.
Connectedness forces every number between $m$ and $M$ into the image.

problems.objective: Use inverse continuity to identify images of relative open intervals.

problems.title: Local continuity does not control a missing boundary
problems.objective: Diagnose a false compactness-style argument on an open domain.
problems.statement: A student argues: “$f(x)=1/x$ is continuous on $(0,1)$, so it is bounded and uniformly continuous there by EVT and Heine-Cantor.” Identify every invalid step and give explicit witnesses to both failed conclusions.
problems.strategy: State that (0,1) is not compact because it is not closed. Then use x_n=1/(n+1) to show f is unbounded. Finally, pair x_n=1/(n+1), y_n=1/(n+2) to show uniform continuity fails.
hints: State that $(0,1)$ is not compact because it is not closed.
Use $x_n=1/(n+1)$ to show $f$ is unbounded.
Pair $x_n=1/(n+1)$, $y_n=1/(n+2)$ to show uniform continuity fails.
problems.solution: EVT and Heine-Cantor require a compact domain; $(0,1)$ is bounded but not closed, hence not compact in $\mathbb R$. Along $x_n=1/(n+1)$, $f(x_n)=n+1$, so $f$ is unbounded. Moreover $|x_n-y_n|\to 0$ for $y_n=1/(n+2)$, while $|f(x_n)-f(y_n)|=1$, so $f$ is not uniformly continuous.
rubricCriteria: Correctly carries out the first key step: State that (0,1) is not compact because it is not closed.
Justifies the central transition: Use x_n=1/(n+1) to show f is unbounded.
Completes the requested conclusion: Pair x_n=1/(n+1), y_n=1/(n+2) to show uniform continuity fails.
